newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal sees budget plan clearing route to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Portugal sees budget plan clearing route to EMU.

text.p: Portugal's minority Socialist government sent its 1997 budget to parliament on Tuesday confident it would "open the doors" for the country to join the European Union's planned single currency.
Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco told a news conference that the government's goal of winning a place for Portugal in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was "clearly attainable."
"The budget opens the doors for us to EMU," he told a news conference to present details of the package.

The budget plan would cut the state deficit to inside the EMU limit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, the year in which aspiring members must meet a series of tough entry tests.
The deficit is forecast to be around four percent in 1996.

Most analysts believe that Portugal has a reasonable chance of making the cut for EMU, when it is formally launched in 1999, and local bond prices have been gaining sharply as international investors begin to bet on it being included.
The budget programme, which was formally approved by the cabinet on Monday night, forecasts a significant rise in government income, although there will be no increase in overall tax levels.

The government is betting on more efficient tax collection and expectations that the Portuguese economy will grow faster than the European average next year to boost its revenues. Faster economic growth automatically generates more income, particularly from indirect taxes.
Severe limits have been clamped on expenditure, with only the Education and Social Security Ministries seeing any increase in the what they can spend.

Although the Socialists of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres are four seats short of an absolute majority in the 230-seat parliament, political analysts see few problems for the government in pushing the budget plan through the legislature.
Guterres has hinted that he would rather resign than see the budget "disfigured" in the legislature.
But the main opposition party, the Social Democrats, who share the Socialists' commitment to Europe, has already said that it is not prepared to see a snap election over the budget.
If the government turned the financial package into a confidence issue, then the Social Democrats would abstain, party leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa has said.
No dates have yet been set for the parliamentary debate, however the budget package is normally approved by mid-December.
But if the government seems to be facing a fairly smooth ride over the budget, the other key element in its economic strategy -- wages -- could pose more problems.
While Portugal looks well-placed to meet the deficit target for EMU entry, it will struggle to make the grade on inflation if it fails to keep a firm lid on wage rises, analysts say.
Unions have reject as a "provocation" an initial government offer of 2.375 percent -- which would be the mid-point of the predicted inflation rate for next year.
